title: The Sneaky Golden Crown
concept: Water rises when something takes up room; equal-weight objects can displace different amounts of water.
legendStatus: The crown-and-bath episode is a legend. It is first recorded by Vitruvius about two centuries after Archimedes and does not appear in Archimedes' own surviving writings.

grownUpFactSupport.claim: The golden-crown story is known only from Vitruvius, not from Archimedes himself.
grownUpFactSupport.detail: Vitruvius tells it in the preface to Book 9 of De architectura; no earlier account survives.

grownUpFactSupport.claim: Vitruvius wrote roughly two hundred years after Archimedes.
grownUpFactSupport.detail: Archimedes lived c. 287-212 BCE; De architectura was written c. 27-23 BCE.

grownUpFactSupport.claim: Pure gold is far denser than pure silver.
grownUpFactSupport.detail: Gold is about 19.3 g/cm3 (19.30) and silver about 10.5 g/cm3 (10.49) near room temperature.

grownUpFactSupport.claim: So an equal-weight crown mixed with silver displaces more water than pure gold.
grownUpFactSupport.detail: Lower density means more volume for the same weight, which raises the waterline higher.

sources.title: Vitruvius, De architectura (On Architecture), Book IX, preface (English translation, LacusCurtius)
sources.note: Earliest surviving source for the golden-crown displacement story.
